title: Share live data without copying it
goal: Explain provider-owned live sharing, then compare Databricks OpenSharing with Snowflake Secure Data Sharing.
concept:
Think of a library card. The library keeps one book; readers receive permission to read it. A shared table works the same way: the provider keeps the governed data and grants read access. The recipient queries the provider-owned data instead of receiving a frozen export.

This removes scheduled copy jobs, but it does not remove authorization, query cost, egress, schema-change risk, or the need to know who may see each row.
example: The fraud team owns risk.daily_scores. A partner needs current scores for five regions. A nightly CSV is twelve hours stale and becomes an unmanaged copy. A share keeps one provider-owned table current; a dynamic view can expose only approved rows and columns.

use_case.when: Use live sharing when another team or organization needs current governed data but should not own an independent extract pipeline.
use_case.example: A bank shares daily risk scores with a claims partner while keeping the source table, policy and audit trail under provider control.
use_case.decision: Choose a live share when freshness and centralized revocation outweigh cross-region egress and provider coupling. Use a materialized export when the recipient needs isolation, offline processing or a stable historical snapshot.

practice: Change the provider version, access state and region. Predict whether the reader sees current rows, stale rows, or no rows.
boundary: The browser model represents one table version and one grant. Real sharing adds identity federation, object eligibility, regions/clouds, billing, auditing, schema evolution and product-specific limitations. Vendor SQL below was not executed.

The recipient automatically becomes owner

One governed object and provider-controlled grants reduce unmanaged copies.
When is an export a better fit?
The consumer needs an isolated historical snapshot
The provider wants immediate revocation
Freshness must be near real time

product_sections.title: Databricks: share a Unity Catalog object
product_sections.html:
Use case. Give a partner read access to a governed table without building a second ingestion pipeline.

Unexecuted vendor practice. Run only in an authorized workspace. The browser visual is a local model.

CREATE SHARE risk_partner;ALTER SHARE risk_partner ADD TABLE risk.daily_scores;CREATE RECIPIENT claims_partner;GRANT SELECT ON SHARE risk_partner TO RECIPIENT claims_partner;

product_sections.title: Snowflake: a share becomes a read-only imported database
product_sections.html:
Use case. Share selected database objects with another Snowflake account without copying their storage.

Unexecuted vendor practice. Use an authorized provider and consumer account. The browser visual is local JavaScript.

CREATE SHARE risk_partner;GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE risk TO SHARE risk_partner;GRANT SELECT ON TABLE risk.public.daily_scores TO SHARE risk_partner;ALTER SHARE risk_partner ADD ACCOUNTS = consumer_org.consumer;-- consumer: CREATE DATABASE risk_shared FROM SHARE provider_org.provider.risk_partner;

Failure/fix. The imported database is read-only; the consumer pays query compute while the provider keeps storage. One share is associated with one database. Use secure views or database roles to narrow exposure; use reader accounts for consumers without Snowflake accounts.

title: One lock order breaks the deadlock cycle
goal: Prevent a two-resource deadlock by requiring every transaction to acquire locks in the same order.
concept:
Two people enter a narrow hallway from opposite ends. Each waits for the other to move. A database deadlock is the same shape: transaction A holds account 7 and waits for 9; transaction B holds 9 and waits for 7.

A consistent lock order removes the circle. If every transfer locks the smaller account ID first, only one transaction can enter the pair; the other waits without holding the second half of a cycle.
example: Transfer T1 moves $10 from account 7 to 9. Transfer T2 moves $5 from 9 to 7. The broken version locks “from” first and deadlocks. The fixed version locks min(7,9) then max(7,9).

use_case.when: Use a lock-order rule when transactions routinely lock more than one shared row or object and deadlocks appear under concurrency.
use_case.example: Two account transfers touch the same pair in opposite directions.
use_case.decision: Prefer a simple global order when the lock set is known. Still catch and retry deadlock victims because dynamic queries, indexes and other code paths can introduce cycles.

practice: Toggle ordered locking and step through both transfers. Find the exact wait-for cycle.
boundary: This deterministic browser schedule illustrates one interleaving. A real database chooses locks from query plans and may deadlock through indexes, predicates or unrelated code. Consistent ordering reduces a class of deadlocks; it does not replace bounded retries.

T2
'+s[1]+'
Result
'+(orderedLocks.checked?'wait chain, no cycle':lockI===1?'7 → 9 → 7':'opposite order')+'

A queue only
A wait-for cycle
A read skew
Each transaction waits for a resource held by the other.
Which rule prevents this two-row cycle?

Both lock the smaller account ID first

A shared total order prevents opposite acquisition order.
Why keep retry logic?
Deadlocks can still arise through other lock paths
Ordering makes commits optional
Retries unlock rows
The rule covers only lock paths that follow it; databases may find other cycles.

title: A 99.9% service cannot make a 99.9% chain
goal: Compose dependency reliability and allocate an end-to-end SLO budget instead of giving every component the user target.
concept:
A trip with two 99%-reliable flights succeeds only when both flights succeed. The chance is roughly 99% × 99% = 98.01%. A request that needs several services behaves the same way when their failures are independent.

The user journey owns the SLO. Component objectives are budget allocations, not copies of the end-to-end number.
example: Checkout requires Orders, Payments and Inventory. At 99.95% each, the independent-path estimate is 0.9995³ = 99.8501%, below a 99.9% checkout target. The design needs stronger components, redundancy, or a degraded path that removes a hard dependency.

use_case.when: Use end-to-end SLO composition when one user action synchronously depends on several services, queues or data stores.
use_case.example: Checkout calls Orders, Payments and Inventory before returning success.
use_case.decision: Model the critical path, measure the actual journey, and allocate component budgets according to leverage. Do not multiply blindly when failures are correlated or fallbacks change the path.

practice: Change dependency count and component availability. Predict the end-to-end estimate and remaining error budget.
boundary: The calculator assumes identical independent availability and a serial all-required path. Real incidents are correlated, latency matters, traffic weights differ, and fallbacks can change the graph. Measure the user SLI; use this only as a planning check.

function paintSlo(){const n=Number(depCount.value),a=Number(depAvail.value)/100,end=Math.pow(a,n)*100,target=99.9,budget=Math.max(0,100-end);sloWorld.innerHTML='

Path: '+Array.from({length:n},(_,i)=>'S'+(i+1)).join(' AND ')+'

Estimated success: '+end.toFixed(4)+'% · failure budget used: '+budget.toFixed(4)+'%

99.9% journey target: '+(end>=target?'fits estimate':'misses estimate')+'

';}depCount.oninput=paintSlo;depAvail.oninput=paintSlo;paintSlo();

title: Compare candidates on the same cases
goal: Build a paired agent evaluation so case difficulty cannot masquerade as a model improvement.
concept:
If two runners use different tracks, the faster time may come from the track. Agent candidates have the same problem: a new prompt tested on easier cases can look better by accident.

A paired eval runs baseline A and candidate B on the same case, reset from the same starting state. Record A win, B win, tie, or both fail. Inspect disagreements; the average alone hides which behavior changed.
example: On five support cases, A passes 3 and B passes 4. The paired table reveals B wins two cases, A wins one, and two tie. The net is +1 case—not “B is 33% better.” Re-run with more representative cases and stable graders.

use_case.when: Use paired evaluations before changing a model, prompt, tool schema, retrieval policy or harness limit.
use_case.example: Compare an existing support agent with a new tool-routing prompt on the same frozen tickets and sandbox snapshots.
use_case.decision: Pair cases and initial state when the question is “did this change help?” Use separate holdouts to detect overfitting and human review for consequential disagreements.

practice: Toggle baseline and candidate outcomes for five cases. Watch wins, losses, ties and net change update.
boundary: The browser counts binary synthetic outcomes. It does not call a model, run tools, estimate statistical significance, validate grader quality, or prevent contamination. Paired results are evidence, not automatic shipping authority.

title: FlashAttention: keep tiles, not the whole attention matrix
goal: Understand how exact tiled attention reduces high-bandwidth-memory traffic without changing the attention result.
concept:
Standard attention compares every query token with every key token. The score grid grows as sequence length squared. Writing that whole grid to slow, large GPU memory and reading it back can dominate runtime.

FlashAttention tiles the grid. It loads small query/key/value blocks into fast on-chip memory, updates a running softmax summary, and discards each score tile. The final answer is exact up to normal floating-point effects; the full score matrix never has to live in high-bandwidth memory.
example: For four query tokens and four key tokens, the conceptual score grid has 16 cells. With a 2×2 tile, the algorithm handles four cells at a time, updates running maximum/sum/output values, then reuses the scratch space.

use_case.when: Use FlashAttention through a supported framework/kernel when long-sequence exact attention is limited by GPU memory traffic.
use_case.example: A transformer processes an 8k-token document and cannot afford to materialize every attention score in HBM.
use_case.decision: Use supported kernels and benchmark your shapes/hardware. It does not make quadratic arithmetic linear, and small or unsupported workloads may not benefit.

practice: Change sequence length and tile size. Compare full score cells with peak teaching-model tile cells.
boundary: This is a memory-shape teaching model, not a GPU kernel. It omits heads, batch, bytes per element, backward pass, kernel fusion, hardware constraints and measured speed. The paper reports experimental claims; production gains depend on implementation and hardware.

'+Array.from({length:Math.min(full,64)},(_,i)=>'
'+(i').join('')+'

Full score cells: '+full+' · peak tile cells in this model: '+tile+' · arithmetic comparisons still '+full+'

';}seqN.oninput=paintFlash;tileN.oninput=paintFlash;paintFlash();

title: A rerun keeps the run ID but increments the attempt
goal: Name logs and deployment evidence with both GitHub Actions run identity and attempt identity.
concept:
A support ticket keeps the same ticket number when reopened, but the reopen count changes. GitHub Actions reruns follow that shape: GITHUB_RUN_ID stays the same, while GITHUB_RUN_ATTEMPT starts at 1 and increments.

If an external dashboard keys only by run ID, a rerun can overwrite the first failure and erase useful evidence.
example: Run 815 fails on attempt 1, then passes on attempt 2. Store evidence as 815/1 and 815/2. The commit SHA stays the same for the rerun, so the comparison isolates environment or nondeterminism rather than a code change.

use_case.when: Use attempt-aware keys whenever workflow reruns publish logs, test reports, metrics or deployment evidence outside GitHub.
use_case.example: A flaky integration job fails, is rerun, and passes without a new commit.
use_case.decision: Keep run ID for the logical workflow execution and append attempt for immutable observations. Do not treat a passing rerun as proof that the first failure was harmless.

practice: Select an attempt and compare the unsafe run-only key with the safe run/attempt key.
boundary: The browser does not run GitHub Actions. Retention, artifact naming conflicts, APIs and permissions differ by workflow. A unique attempt key preserves evidence but does not diagnose why attempts disagree.

title: A field mask says exactly what PATCH may change
goal: Use FieldMask to distinguish an omitted field from an intentional clear or default value.
concept:
A repair form has two parts: the new value and a checklist of which rooms workers may enter. Sending display_name: "" without the checklist is ambiguous—is it an intentional clear or a serialization default?

A field mask is that checklist. The server changes only listed paths. Values outside the mask are ignored or rejected by contract, so adding future fields does not accidentally erase them.
example: Current user: {name: "Kai", timezone: "UTC", alerts: true}. Request body sends {timezone: "America/New_York", alerts: false} with mask timezone. Only timezone changes; alerts stays true.

use_case.when: Use field masks for partial updates when resources have optional/default values, nested fields, or will evolve with new fields.
use_case.example: A profile client changes timezone without overwriting alert settings added by a newer server.
use_case.decision: Use PATCH plus an explicit update mask for selective change. Use full replacement only when clients intentionally own every field and concurrency control protects lost updates.

practice: Select a mask and payload. Predict the resource after the patch, including an intentional clear.
boundary: This local model supports flat fields only. Real protobuf FieldMask paths can be nested and have rules for repeated/map fields, immutable fields, wildcards, unknown paths, validation, etags and authorization.

It stays unchanged
The field is deleted
Only paths named in the mask participate in the update.
How do you intentionally clear display_name?
Omit it
Include display_name in the mask and send its clear/default value

Mask membership carries intent; the value carries the new state.
Why is full replacement risky as schemas evolve?
Older clients may overwrite fields they do not know
PATCH cannot be authorized

An older client cannot preserve unknown fields if it replaces the whole resource.
